Learning Japanese with Silhouette (Naruto Shippuden Opening) 🧵

Oikakeru, kage, and how te iku encodes the direction that Sasuke is always going

Silhouette is written in Japanese as シルエット (shirueetto), a katakana loanword from the English (originally French) word. It means the same thing: the dark outline or shadow-form of a figure seen against a lighter background.

Did you already know any of these? Reply 👇

Oikakeru (追いかける) means to chase after, to pursue, to run after someone. It combines oi- (the combining form of 追う, to chase) with kakeru (駆ける, to run, to race). The compound: to run in active pursuit.

Kakete iku (駆けていく) means to run off and keep going, to race away. It combines kakeru (駆ける, to run, to race) in te-form with iku (to go). The iku encodes direction: the action is moving away from the current speaker's position.

Raikou, Entei, and Suicune - The Three Pokémon Ho-Oh Brought Back from the Dead 🧵

Lightning struck the Brass Tower. Fire consumed it. Rain put it out. Ho-Oh gave each force to a different beast - and their Japanese names say exactly which.

The six kanji that name these beasts appear throughout anime and lyrics. 雷 (rai) means thunder or lightning — the same character in Raijin, Japan's thunder god. 炎 (en) means flame or blaze — hotter and more literary than everyday 火 (hi). 水 (sui) means water.

Raikou (ライコウ) is built from 雷 (rai) meaning thunder or lightning, and 光 (kou) meaning light. Thunder Light. The lightning bolt that struck the Brass Tower and started everything - that is Raikou's entire identity compressed into two characters.

These kanji compound throughout Japanese vocabulary. 雷雨 (raiu) means thunderstorm — 雨 means rain. 炎上 (enjou) means internet firestorm or burning up. 水泳 (suiei) means swimming. 光年 (kounen) means light-year. 帝国 (teikoku) means empire — 国 means country.

Learning Japanese with Blue Bird (Naruto Shippuden Opening) 🧵

Mama, todoku, and the precise vocabulary for chasing someone who keeps getting further away

Blue Bird is 青い鳥 (aoi tori) in Japanese. Aoi (青い) means blue or blue-green - a colour word in Japanese that traditionally spans sky blue through spring green. Tori (鳥) means bird.

Which one surprised you most? Drop it below 👇

Jiyuu no tori ni nareru (自由の鳥になれる) means "I can become a bird of freedom." Jiyuu (自由) is freedom. の connects it as a modifier: bird of freedom. Ni nareru is the potential form of ni naru (to become something) - can become, not will become.
Mama (まま) as a grammar pattern means "remaining in the state of" or "while unchanged." It attaches to a past verb form (た-form) for completed states or a negative form (ない-form) for ongoing absences.

How English loanwords written in katakana give you a massive head start

Japanese actually uses three writing systems simultaneously. Kanji (漢字) are the complex characters borrowed from Chinese - the ones that look like small pictures, like 愛 (love) or 剣 (sword).

Save this for your next rewatch 📸

The linguistic term for these borrowed words is gairaigo (外来語), literally "words that came from outside." They show up constantly in modern Japanese: in everyday conversation, in anime, in product names, in J-pop lyrics.

外来語 (gairaigo) means foreign-origin words — 外 means outside, 来 means to come, 語 means word or language. Japanese borrows from English, Dutch, French, and Portuguese, writing loanwords in カタカナ (katakana).

Kowarekake, identity collapse, and why shiroi repeated eight times is a lesson about dissociation

Kowarekake (壊れかけ) means on the verge of breaking or nearly broken. It uses the auxiliary verb 〜kakeru attached to the masu-stem of 壊れる (to break or be damaged) - koware + kakeru.

Tabete ii yo (食べていいよ) means "it's okay to eat me" or "you can eat me." Taberu is to eat. The te-form tabete + いい (ii, okay/allowed) + よ (yo, assertion particle) creates the standard permissive construction in Japanese.

Shiroi (白い) means white. In Unravel it is repeated eight times in succession. In Japanese culture, white is associated with purity, emptiness, and death - it is the colour of mourning garments and funeral rites.

Deai (出会い) is one of those Japanese words with no perfect English equivalent. The closest is "fateful encounter" or "chance meeting that matters" - but even that is too wordy. Japanese encodes the specialness of the encounter directly in the word.
Deai (出会い) means encounter or meeting - specifically the noun form of deau (出会う, to meet by chance), which carries more weight than ordinary au (会う, to meet). A deai is not a scheduled appointment.

Shunkan (瞬間) means moment or instant - a specific, precise point in time rather than a duration. The characters 瞬 (blink/instant) + 間 (interval) create: the interval of a blink, the smallest possible slice of time.

Learning Japanese with Gurenge (Demon Slayer Opening) 🧵

The hodo pattern, lotus symbolism, and what 'hope seized with trembling hands' really means

Gurenge (紅蓮華) means Red Lotus Flower. The character 紅 (gu/kurenai) means deep red or crimson. 蓮 (ren) is the lotus plant. 華 (ge/hana) means flower or blossom - specifically beautiful, elegant flowering.

Save this for your next rewatch 📸

Tsuyoku nare (強くなれ) means "Become strong!" or "Be strong!" Tsuyoku is the adverbial form of 強い (tsuyoi, strong). Nare is the bare imperative of なる (naru, to become). It is a direct command without any politeness suffix - forceful and intentional.

Senmei ni hikatteru (鮮明に光ってる) means "shining vividly" or "glowing with clarity." Senmei (鮮明) is an N2 adjective meaning vivid, clear, sharply distinct - used for images or memories that stand out with unusual sharpness. Ni makes it adverbial.
